name: SLIM (Smart Lander for Investigating Moon)
short_status: Landed Jan 20, 2024 (JST): world's first pinpoint lunar landing (~10 m vs 100 m goal); survived three lunar nights; operations ended Aug 23, 2024.
tagline: JAXA · Japan · Lander · 2024 · Commercial and multipolar Success
stats: pinpoint landing accuracy, possibly 3-4 m, against a 100 m goal
dry mass: the lightest successful lunar lander per JAXA
survived, with zero night-survival design requirement
country to soft-land on the Moon

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: 7 Sep 2023 (JST), H-IIA Launch Vehicle No. 47 from Tanegashima, ridesharing with the XRISM X-ray telescope

facts.label: Landing
facts.value: 20 Jan 2024 at 00:20 JST (Jan 19, 15:20 UTC / 10:20 a.m. EST); Japan became the fifth country to soft-land on the Moon

facts.label: Landing site
facts.value: 13.3160 S, 25.2510 E (ME coordinates, NASA LRO team), elevation -912 m, on ejecta near the 270 m Shioli crater in Mare Nectaris

facts.label: Pinpoint accuracy
facts.value: Position error at the 50 m altitude checkpoint (before obstacle avoidance took precedence) evaluated at approximately 10 m or less, possibly about 3-4 m; final touchdown about 55 m east of the original target (refined to about 60 m in the Dec 2024 project review)

facts.label: Main engine anomaly
facts.value: At about 50 m altitude the -X main engine's ceramic nozzle separated and thrust dropped; autonomous software continued descent on one engine, drifting east; touchdown vertical speed was 1.4 m/s or less but lateral velocity and attitude exceeded design limits, leaving SLIM nose-down with solar cells facing west

facts.label: Root cause (published Dec 26, 2024)
facts.value: Blowdown propellant feed pressure was low late in flight; simultaneous firing of the 12 auxiliary thrusters at main-engine ignition transiently dropped supply pressure, the -X engine failed to ignite for about 1 second, then unburned accumulated propellant lit with an excessive ignition shock that detached the nozzle; anomaly occurred at ~98% of total propulsion from separation to landing

facts.label: Rovers
facts.value: LEV-1 (2.1 kg, hopping locomotion, own direct-to-Earth comms) and LEV-2 'SORA-Q' (238 g, ~8 cm, developed with Takara Tomy, Sony Group and Doshisha University; world's smallest and lightest lunar exploration robot per JAXA) separated successfully just before touchdown; JAXA calls it the world's first lunar exploration by coordinated multiple robots

facts.label: The famous photo
facts.value: The nose-down image of SLIM was taken by LEV-2 (SORA-Q) and sent to LEV-1 by short-range (Bluetooth) link, then relayed to Earth by LEV-1

facts.label: Power recovery and science
facts.value: Shut down at 02:57 JST on landing night; resumed operations 28 Jan 2024 when the sun angle changed; Multi-Band Camera then made 10-band near-infrared spectral observations of 10 rocks (dog-breed nicknames such as Toy Poodle and AKITAINU) plus 2 regolith sites, exceeding expectations, targeting olivine chemistry relevant to lunar mantle composition

facts.label: Lunar nights survived
facts.value: Three, despite no night-survival design requirement; post-night comm windows were Feb 25-Mar 1, Mar 27-30, and 23-29 Apr 2024; last contact 28 Apr 2024

facts.label: Laser ranging
facts.value: On 24 May 2024, NASA's LRO bounced laser pulses off SLIM's 2-inch NASA Laser Retroreflector Array (~21 g) on two successive orbits from ~70 km altitude, despite the array lying sideways; SLIM remains a passive laser target on the surface for decades

facts.label: End of operations
facts.value: 23 Aug 2024 at 22:40 JST, after re-contact attempts from May through July failed (announced 26 Aug 2024)

facts.label: Spacecraft
facts.value: Approx. 200 kg dry / 715 kg at launch; ~2.4 m x 1.7 m x 2.7 m; JAXA assesses SLIM as the lightest successful lunar lander; total project development cost 14.9 billion yen

facts.label: Success grading
facts.value: 26 Dec 2024 project review: minimum success, full success, and extra success criteria all achieved

facts.label: Legacy
facts.value: Image-matching navigation feeds JAXA's MMX Mars-moons mission; Multi-Band Camera technology transfers to the ALIS spectrometer on the LUPEX rover with ISRO; flight results paper (Sakai et al.) published in Acta Astronautica vol. 235, Oct 2025

timeline: SLIM becomes a JAXA project (concept lineage back to SELENE-B studies from 2002)
Launch on H-IIA No. 47 from Tanegashima, with XRISM
Touchdown at 00:20 JST near Shioli crater after releasing LEV-1 and LEV-2 seconds earlier; world's first pinpoint lunar landing despite nozzle loss at 50 m; powered down 02:57 JST to preserve battery
NASA's LRO images SLIM on the surface from ~80 km (published Jan 26)
Operations resume as the sun reaches the west-facing solar cells; Multi-Band Camera science runs until lunar sunset (~Jan 31)
Survives three lunar nights (comm windows Feb 25-Mar 1, Mar 27-30, Apr 23-29)
LRO successfully laser-ranges SLIM's NASA retroreflector on two successive orbits
JAXA terminates SLIM operations at 22:40 JST after months of failed re-contact attempts (announced Aug 26)
Project review: minimum, full, and extra success all achieved; nozzle-separation root cause published
Definitive flight-results paper (Sakai et al.) appears in Acta Astronautica vol. 235
